english: Happy New Year (lit. receive many blessings)
usage: Happy New Year (please receive many blessings)
Polite default; say to elders, bosses, anyone you respect at New Year
반말, to close friends and younger people
합쇼체; very formal, to a CEO, in a speech, or a written card
Shortened; also used at 추석 and other holidays, not just New Year
examples: A: 새해 복 많이 받으세요! / B: 감사합니다, 선생님도 새해 복 많이 받으세요.
A: Happy New Year! / B: Thank you, I wish you the same.
The expected reciprocal exchange — you mirror the phrase back to show respect
할머니, 새해 복 많이 받으세요. 건강하세요.
Grandma, Happy New Year. Stay healthy.
Add 건강하세요 ('stay healthy') to an elder — the most-wished thing for grandparents
올해도 잘 부탁드립니다. 새해 복 많이 받으세요.
I look forward to working with you this year too. Happy New Year.
A polite work/colleague version pairing the greeting with 잘 부탁드립니다
nuance: 새해 복 많이 받으세요 literally means 'in the new year, please RECEIVE much 복 (blessing/fortune)' — 복 is a Sino-Korean word (福) for luck and good fortune, and the verb is 받다 ('to receive'), so you are wishing that blessings come TO the person. This is the single most important holiday phrase in Korea, said on 설날 (Lunar New Year) to virtually everyone: elders, bosses, neighbors, shop owners. The default register is the 세요 form (honorific), safe for anyone older or not close; with friends and kids you drop to 새해 복 많이 받아; in a formal speech or written card, 받으십시오 (합쇼체) is more weighty. The huge English-speaker pitfall is the verb direction: learners say 새해 복 많이 주세요 ('please GIVE me blessings'), but 주다 ('give') flips it so you are asking blessings for yourself — which sounds absurd. It must be 받으세요. A second trap is translating the English word 'happy' (행복) — 행복한 새해 보내세요 sounds like translated English; the true fixed idiom is the 복 받으세요 formula. The nearest near-synonym expression is 행운을 빌어요 ('I wish you luck'), but that is a general year-round phrase that cannot substitute for this specific New Year formula. Note it shortens to 복 많이 받으세요 at 추석 and other holidays too, and when greeting an elder you typically combine it with a 세배 (deep bow).

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'in the new year, please receive much 복 (福 = blessing/fortune)'. The verb 받다 ('receive') means blessings flow TO the listener — you are wishing them a fortune-filled year, not asking for anything yourself. It is the single most important holiday expression in Korea.
복 is Sino-Korean 福, meaning luck, good fortune, and well-being — a cornerstone concept in Korean holiday culture.

Said at 설날 (Lunar New Year) to almost everyone. Default polite form 받으세요 works for elders, bosses, neighbors; drop to 받아 for close friends and children; use 받으십시오 in speeches or formal written cards. Also fine for 추석 and other holidays in shortened form 복 많이 받으세요.
새해 복 많이 받으세요 → 복 많이 받으세요 (shortened, multi-holiday) → 새해 복 많이 받아 (반말 friends) → 새해 복 많이 받으십시오 (합쇼체 formal). Elders are greeted with a 세배 (deep bow) accompanying the phrase.
새해 복 많이 받으세요 is specifically for major holidays (설날/추석). For any season you might say 행운을 빌어요 ('I wish you luck'), but that phrase does NOT replace this fixed New Year formula.

Two traps: (1) 주세요 instead of 받으세요 — 주다 ('give') reverses the direction so you ask blessings for yourself, which sounds selfish. (2) Inserting 행복: 행복한 새해 보내세요 mirrors English 'Have a Happy New Year' but sounds translated. The authentic Korean formula is the 복 받으세요 structure, not a 행복 construction.

mistakes: Saying 새해 복 많이 주세요.
주다 means 'give', so this asks the listener to give YOU fortune — backwards and comical. The blessing flows toward the listener, so use 받다: 새해 복 많이 받으세요.
Translating literally as 행복한 새해 (보내세요).
Korean doesn't use 행복한 ('happy') for the New Year greeting; the set idiom is the 복 받으세요 formula. 행복한 새해 sounds like translated English.
Using 받아 with your boss or an elder.
받아 is 반말 and too casual for someone you should respect. Keep the honorific 받으세요; only drop to 받아 with friends and younger people.

english: I'll do the New Year bow for you
usage: I'll bow to you (New Year bow)
Polite-humble; announce it to an elder before you bow
Please receive my New Year bow
Said by some as they begin; lit. 'receive the bow'
I'll do my New Year bow
반말, to family elders you're close with
I will now perform the New Year bow
Formal; in a more ceremonial family setting
examples: 할아버지, 세배 드릴게요.
Grandpa, let me do my New Year bow for you.
Said as you kneel down in front of an elder on 설날 morning — the standard announcement before bowing
A: 세배 드릴게요. 새해 복 많이 받으세요. / B: 그래, 새해 복 많이 받아라. 자, 세뱃돈이야.
A: I'll bow to you. Happy New Year. / B: Yes, Happy New Year to you too. Here's your New Year money.
The complete exchange: bow → New Year wish → elder replies with 덕담 and hands 세뱃돈
애들아, 할머니께 세배 드려.
Kids, do your New Year bow to Grandma.
A parent prompting children; note 께 (honorific 'to') for Grandma
nuance: 세배 (歲拜) is the deep, kneeling New Year bow younger people give to elders on 설날, and 드리다 is the humble verb for 'to give (to a superior)' — so 세배 드릴게요 is literally 'I'll give you a New Year bow (humbly)', the polite announcement before bowing. The verb choice is fundamental: you 드리다 (humbly give) a 세배 UP to an elder, and the elder 받다 (receives) it, then typically replies with a 덕담 (blessing, kind wishes for your year) and hands the younger person 세뱃돈 (New Year money). The big English-speaker pitfall is using the plain verb 주다 instead of the humble 드리다: 세배 줄게요 is wrong because 주다 is not humble enough toward an elder; to anyone you bow to, use 드리다. A second trap is the particle: elders take the honorific directional 께, not the casual 한테 (세배 할머니한테 드려요 → should be 할머니께 드려요). Don't confuse 세배 (the Lunar New Year bow to a living elder) with 절 (a bow in general, including at funerals or in front of an ancestral tablet) — all 세배 are a type of 절, but 세배 is exclusively the New Year ritual.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'I will give you a 세배 (歲拜 = New Year bow)'. 세배 (歲拜) means a bow specific to the New Year; 드리다 is the humble verb 'to give to a superior'. The phrase announces you are about to perform this bow, inviting the elder to receive it.

Used on the morning of 설날 before kneeling. Always with an elder (parents, grandparents, relatives). The -ㄹ게요 form (polite intention) is standard; 드리겠습니다 is more ceremonial. Never say it to a peer or someone younger — the bow only goes upward.

세배 (New Year bow to living elder) vs 절 (bow in any ritual: funeral, ancestral rite, general respect) — all 세배 are 절 but not vice versa. Using 절 드릴게요 at the New Year is understood but less specific than 세배 드릴게요.
세배 드릴게요 → 세배 드리겠습니다 (more formal) → 세배할게 (반말). After bowing you add the New Year greeting: 새해 복 많이 받으세요. The elder responds with a 덕담 and typically gives 세뱃돈 (New Year money).

Two traps: (1) 주다 vs 드리다 — 세배 줄게요 fails because 주다 is a plain give-verb, not humble enough toward an elder who deserves the humble form 드리다. (2) Particle: elders require 께 (할머니께), not the casual 한테 (할머니한테) used for peers and friends.

mistakes: Saying 세배 줄게요 to an elder.
주다 isn't humble enough when the recipient is someone you respect. The humble give-verb is 드리다: 세배 드릴게요.
Using 한테 instead of 께: 할머니한테 세배.
한테 is casual 'to'; for an elder use the honorific 께: 할머니께 세배 드려요. 한테 sounds disrespectful in this ritual context.
Calling every bow 세배.
세배 is specifically the New Year bow to elders. The bows to ancestors (차례) or at a funeral are just 절, not 세배. Reserve 세배 for 설날.

english: Did you have tteokguk? (Did you celebrate New Year?)
usage: Polite; warm small-talk at New Year, 드셨- is the honorific past of 먹다 ('ate')
Offering a bowl to a guest; 그릇 = 'bowl' counter
Guess you're a year older now
The joke that follows — eating tteokguk 'adds a year'
examples: A: 떡국 드셨어요? / B: 네, 아침에 먹었어요. 벌써 한 살 더 먹었네요!
A: Did you have tteokguk? / B: Yes, had it this morning. I've aged a year already!
The classic New Year A/B exchange — question triggers the 한 살 더 먹다 joke
새해 복 많이 받으세요. 떡국 드셨어요?
Happy New Year. Did you have tteokguk?
A natural pairing — the greeting plus this friendly New Year question
저 오늘 떡국 두 그릇 먹었어요. 두 살 먹었나 봐요.
I had two bowls of tteokguk today — guess I aged two years.
A playful reply leaning into the 'tteokguk = +1 year' idea; 두 그릇 = two bowls
nuance: 떡국 is the rice-cake soup Koreans eat on 설날 morning, and there's a deep cultural belief that eating a bowl of 떡국 makes you a year older — so 떡국 드셨어요? ('did you have tteokguk?') is really a warm, idiomatic way of asking 'did you celebrate / welcome in the New Year?'. It is light small-talk, not a literal nutrition question; the expected move is to smile and play along. 드셨어요 is the honorific past of 먹다 (먹다 → 드시다 → 드셨어요), so use it for elders and strangers; with friends drop to 떡국 먹었어?. The follow-up joke is 한 살 더 먹었네요 ('you ate one more year of age') — note Korean uses the verb 먹다 ('eat') for gaining age: 나이를 먹다. The English-speaker pitfall is taking it literally and answering only about the food, missing the New-Year-greeting subtext. A second trap is register inconsistency: if you ask 떡국 드셨어요? (honorific) but then joke 한 살 더 먹었네 (반말), the levels clash — keep it 드셨네요 to an elder. Do not confuse 떡국 (New Year rice-cake soup) with 떡볶이 (spicy stir-fried rice cakes) — completely different dishes.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'Did you eat 떡국 (rice-cake soup)?'. Real meaning: 'Did you celebrate the New Year / have you become a year older?' — because eating 떡국 on 설날 morning is said to add a year to your age. The food question is purely a cultural stand-in for a New Year greeting.

Classic New Year small-talk, January/February during the 설날 period. 드셨어요 (honorific past) for elders/strangers; 먹었어? (반말) for close friends. Inappropriate outside the New Year context — asking this in March about a random lunch would just seem odd.

At Chuseok the equivalent cultural-food question is 송편 드셨어요? ('did you have songpyeon?'). Both are warm, culturally loaded food-as-greeting patterns. 떡국 vs 떡볶이 are entirely different foods — do not confuse them.
떡국 드셨어요? → 떡국 먹었어? (반말) → 떡국 한 그릇 드세요 (offering). Natural follow-up: 한 살 더 드셨네요 (polite) / 한 살 더 먹었네 (casual). Counter: 한 그릇 = one bowl, 두 그릇 = two bowls.

Two traps: (1) Answering literally — saying just 'yes, I had soup' without engaging with the 한 살 더 먹다 age-joke loses all the cultural warmth; play along. (2) Register clash: mixing 드셨어요? with a 반말 follow-up (한 살 더 먹었네) when speaking to an elder sounds jarring. Keep the register consistent throughout.

mistakes: Answering only literally about the food.
떡국 드셨어요? at New Year carries the 'are you a year older / did you celebrate' meaning. Engage with the 한 살 더 먹다 joke rather than just saying whether you ate.
Using 먹었어요 instead of honorific 드셨어요 with an elder.
먹다's honorific is 드시다. To an elder or stranger say 떡국 드셨어요?; 먹었어요 is fine only with peers, and 먹었어? only with friends.
Saying 나이를 받다 for getting older.
Korean gains age with the verb 먹다: 한 살 더 먹다. 나이를 받다 ('receive age') is wrong — you 'eat' a year of age.

usage: Polite default; said before 설날/추석 to almost anyone
연휴 ('consecutive days off') focuses on the holiday break itself
Swap in the specific holiday name when you know which one
examples: A: 명절 잘 보내세요! / B: 감사합니다, 과장님도 명절 잘 보내세요.
A: Have a good holiday! / B: Thank you, you too, manager.
The workplace farewell before the holiday — always mirror it back politely
미리 명절 잘 보내세요!
Have a good holiday in advance!
미리 ('in advance') is added when you say it a day or two before the holiday
연휴 동안 푹 쉬세요. 명절 잘 보내세요.
Rest well during the break. Have a good holiday.
푹 쉬세요 ('rest well') is a kind add-on for the holiday break
nuance: 명절 is the word for a traditional Korean holiday — specifically the big two, 설날 (Lunar New Year) and 추석 (Chuseok/harvest festival) — and 잘 보내세요 means 'spend (it) well', from 보내다 ('to spend/pass time'). So 명절 잘 보내세요 is the standard 'have a good holiday' said to coworkers, neighbors, and shopkeepers in the days BEFORE the holiday. The crucial contrast is 명절 vs 연휴: 명절 names the cultural holiday with its rituals (제사, 차례, 성묘), while 연휴 just means the consecutive days off — say 연휴 잘 보내세요 when you mean 'enjoy the long weekend' generically (works for any holiday block including modern ones). Adding 미리 ('in advance') is very common because people scatter to their hometowns right before the holiday. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb: learners reach for 가지세요 ('have/possess') as a 직역 of English 'have a good holiday', but Korean uses 보내다 ('spend/pass'); 명절 가지세요 is wrong. A second pitfall is timing — 잘 보내세요 is for BEFORE the holiday; afterward you switch to the past 명절 잘 보내셨어요? ('did you have a good holiday?').

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'spend the holiday well'. 보내다 means 'to pass/spend time', so the phrase literally invites the listener to spend the holiday period pleasurably. The word 명절 specifically names a traditional Korean holiday (설날, 추석), not any generic day off.

Said in the days leading up to 설날 or 추석 to coworkers, neighbors, shopkeepers — basically anyone you interact with. Polite 보내세요 is the default; 보내 for close friends. Add the specific holiday name (설날 잘 보내세요 / 추석 잘 보내세요) when you want to be more specific.

명절 잘 보내세요 (cultural holiday with rituals) vs 연휴 잘 보내세요 (just the days-off block). Use 명절 when the cultural/family dimension matters; use 연휴 for any long weekend including modern public holidays that aren't traditional.
명절 잘 보내세요 → 미리 명절 잘 보내세요 (in advance) → 명절 잘 보내셨어요? (past, after the holiday). Companions: 푹 쉬세요 ('rest well'), 고향 잘 다녀오세요 ('travel safely to your hometown').

Two traps: (1) Wrong verb — learners try 명절 가지세요 (직역 of 'have a holiday') but 가지다 means 'possess'; use 보내다. (2) Timing mismatch — 보내세요 (future) is for before the holiday; after it ends use the past form 명절 잘 보내셨어요? Saying 보내세요 after the holiday has passed sounds strange.

mistakes: Saying 명절 가지세요 ('have a holiday').
Korean uses 보내다 ('spend/pass time'), not 가지다 ('possess'). The set phrase is 명절 잘 보내세요. 가지세요 is a direct-translation error.
Confusing 명절 with 연휴.
명절 is the cultural holiday (설날/추석); 연휴 is just the string of days off. For a generic long weekend say 연휴 잘 보내세요; for the traditional holiday, 명절.
Saying 잘 보내세요 after the holiday is over.
보내세요 (future) wishes a good holiday ahead. After it's done, switch to past: 명절 잘 보내셨어요? ('did you have a good holiday?').

usage: 반말, asking a friend if their family does it
Add -러 가다 for 'going in order to'
제사 = the death-anniversary rite; 차례 is the holiday version
examples: A: 설날에 차례 지내세요? / B: 저희 집은 기독교라 대신 추도 예배를 드려요.
A: Do you hold charye on Seollal? / B: Our family is Christian, so we have a memorial service instead.
Shows it's natural to ask — not all families observe 차례
내일 아침 일찍 차례 지내고 성묘 가요.
Tomorrow we do charye early then visit the graves.
차례 (home rite) often pairs with 성묘 ('visiting ancestors' graves')
요즘은 차례 간소하게 지내는 집도 많아요.
These days many families keep charye simple.
간소하게 ('simply') reflects the modern trend of scaling it down
nuance: 차례 (茶禮) is the ancestral memorial rite families perform on the morning of 설날 and 추석 — food is set on a table for the ancestors and the family bows together. The crucial collocation is the verb: you 지내다 a rite, never 하다. 지내다 here means 'to observe/hold (a ceremony)', and it is the required verb for both 차례 지내다 and 제사 지내다; using 차례 해요 marks you instantly as a learner. The key contrast is 차례 vs 제사: 차례 is the simpler rite tied to the two big HOLIDAYS (always in the morning, shorter food setup), while 제사 is the memorial held on the ANNIVERSARY of a specific ancestor's death (traditionally late at night). The English-speaker pitfall, beyond the verb, is assuming every Korean family holds 차례 — increasingly families simplify (간소화) or skip it entirely, and many Christian families hold a 추도 예배 (memorial worship) instead. It's polite to ask 차례 지내세요? rather than assume. Pair words: 성묘 (visiting graves) and 벌초 (clearing weeds from the grave before Chuseok), which often follow 차례.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'we hold 차례 (茶禮)'. 차례 is an ancestral rite — food is laid out for the ancestors and the family bows. The phrase describes a ritual event, not a casual activity, so 지내다 ('observe/hold a ceremony') is the required verb.

Used on 설날 and 추석 mornings. The rite is family-internal; when talking about it to others, polite 지내요 is standard. It's natural to ask friends whether their family holds it — 차례 지내세요? — since practice varies. Christian families often don't observe it.

차례 (holiday rite: 설날/추석, morning, family-holiday-focused) vs 제사 (death-anniversary rite, traditionally late at night, for one specific ancestor's passing date). Don't use them interchangeably — the timing, occasion, and food setup differ.
차례 지내다 → 차례 지내러 가다 (going to attend) → 차례 간소하게 지내다 (simplify the rite) → 차례 안 지내다 (not observing it). Related: 성묘 가다 (grave visit), 벌초하다 (cut grave weeds).

The biggest trap is using 하다 instead of 지내다: 차례 해요 sounds wrong to every native speaker. Memorial and ancestral rites require 지내다. Beyond the verb, assuming all Koreans do 차례 can be socially awkward — ask rather than state, since many modern families simplify or skip it.

mistakes: Saying 차례 해요 instead of 차례 지내요.
Rituals take the verb 지내다, not 하다. It's 차례(를) 지내다, 제사(를) 지내다. 차례 해요 sounds wrong to natives.
Confusing 차례 with 제사.
차례 is the rite on the holidays (설날/추석), held in the morning. 제사 is the rite on an ancestor's death anniversary, traditionally at night. They're not interchangeable.
Assuming everyone holds 차례.
Many families simplify or skip it, and Christian families often hold a 추도 예배 instead. Ask 차례 지내세요? rather than assuming.

english: We make songpyeon (shape the rice cakes)
usage: Polite-neutral; 빚다 is the verb for shaping rice cakes by hand
같이 ('together') — it's a family group activity
Same verb 빚다 for dumplings, common at 설날
examples: A: 오늘 추석 준비하세요? / B: 네, 가족들이랑 같이 송편 빚고 있어요.
A: Preparing for Chuseok today? / B: Yes, I'm making songpyeon with the family.
Shows 같이 빚다 as a group activity — a real holiday scenario
송편 예쁘게 빚으면 예쁜 딸 낳는대요.
They say if you shape pretty songpyeon you'll have a pretty daughter.
A famous old saying that comes up every Chuseok — a gentle tease while shaping
저는 송편 빚는 거 잘 못해서 모양이 엉망이에요.
I'm bad at shaping songpyeon, so mine look a mess.
엉망이에요 ('a mess') — a relatable thing to say while helping
nuance: 송편 are the small half-moon-shaped rice cakes stuffed with sesame, beans, or chestnut that Koreans make for 추석 (Chuseok). The verb is the specific 빚다 — used for things you shape with your hands from dough or clay: you 빚다 송편, 빚다 만두 (dumplings), and even 빚다 (brew) traditional liquor. You do NOT use 만들다 ('make') for the ritual shaping; 송편 빚어요 captures the hands-together, generational bonding aspect. 빚다 is a regular consonant-stem verb: 빚다 → 빚어요, 빚으면, 빚는 — learners often trip on the stem-final ㅈ. Culturally, making 송편 together the evening before Chuseok is a bonding activity across generations, hence the famous saying 송편 예쁘게 빚으면 예쁜 딸을 낳는다 ('shape pretty songpyeon and you'll have a pretty daughter'). The nearest synonym situation: 만들다 (make generally) is understood but loses the hand-shaping, ritual warmth. The English-speaker pitfall is defaulting to 만들다 for everything; the second pitfall is mixing up Chuseok food 송편 with the New Year food 떡국 — each holiday has its signature dish. Note 빚 (same sound) also means 'debt' — an entirely different word.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'we 빚다 songpyeon'. 빚다 means to shape/mold by hand — the verb implies a deliberate, hands-on craft process. It carries a connotation of care and artisanship that 만들다 ('make') does not, which is why 빚다 is the idiomatic choice for these rice cakes.

Said at home the evening before 추석, as a family activity. Casual register is common since it's a domestic setting: 빚어요 (polite), 빚자 (let's, 반말), 같이 빚어요 (together). You can also describe it to outsiders: 추석 준비로 송편 빚고 있어요 ('making songpyeon in prep for Chuseok').

송편 빚어요 (hand-shape with ritual warmth) vs 송편 만들어요 (make, neutral). Both are understood, but 빚다 is the native choice. Compare: 만두 빚어요 (same verb for dumplings, set phrase). Do not confuse 송편 (Chuseok) with 떡국 (Seollal/New Year) — different holidays, different foods.
송편 빚다 → 같이 빚다 (make together) → 예쁘게 빚다 (shape nicely) → 빚는 거 잘 못하다 ('bad at shaping'). Conjugation reminder: 빚어요, 빚으면, 빚는 (attach to 빚- stem).

Two traps: (1) Defaulting to 만들다 — while understood, it loses the cultural warmth; 빚다 is what natives say. (2) Holiday food confusion —송편 is 추석 (Chuseok), 떡국 is 설날 (New Year). Saying 설날에 송편 빚어요 pairs the wrong food with the wrong holiday and will confuse Koreans.

mistakes: Saying 송편 만들어요 in the ritual context.
Native speakers use the hand-shaping verb 빚다 for songpyeon and dumplings: 송편 빚어요. 만들다 ('make') is understood but less idiomatic here.
Mangling the conjugation (빚다 → 빚다요/빚는다요).
빚다 conjugates 빚어요, 빚으면, 빚는. Attach endings to the 빚 stem (빚-어요), not the dictionary form; 빚어요 is the polite present.
Mixing up holiday foods: 송편 at New Year.
송편 is the 추석 (Chuseok) food; 떡국 is the 설날 (New Year) food. Pair the right rice cake with the right holiday.

usage: Polite-neutral; 입다 is the verb for wearing clothes on the body
입고 가다 ('go while wearing') for showing up dressed in it
한 벌 = the counter for a set/suit of clothes
examples: 설날에 한복 입고 세배해요.
On Seollal we wear hanbok and do the New Year bow.
한복 + 세배 — the classic New Year morning image
A: 돌잔치에 한복 입고 가요? / B: 아, 저는 그냥 정장 입고 갈 것 같아요.
A: Are you going to the first-birthday party in hanbok? / B: Oh, I'll probably just wear a suit.
A realistic exchange — shows hanbok is now optional even at celebrations
애기 한복 입혀서 사진 찍었어요.
We dressed the baby in hanbok and took photos.
입히다 ('dress someone') — the causative, since you put it ON the baby
nuance: 한복 (韓服) is traditional Korean dress, worn for 설날, 추석, weddings, 돌잔치 (first-birthday parties), and palace photo tours. The verb is 입다 ('to wear/put on the torso/body') — Korean splits 'wear' by body part: 입다 for clothes/garments, 쓰다 for hats/glasses, 신다 for shoes/socks, 끼다 for rings/gloves, 차다 for watches/accessories. A 직역 of English 'wear' with one verb is a classic error; for 한복 it is always 입다. The important causative is 입히다 ('to dress someone'): you 입다 your own 한복 but 입히다 a child's hanbok (한복 입혔어요), which learners routinely miss. Wearing hanbok on holidays used to be near-universal but is now optional — many families wear regular clothes, and renting (빌리다) a 한복 for palace photos is now very popular with tourists and young Koreans alike. The English-speaker pitfall beyond the wear-verb split is the counter: a hanbok outfit is counted with 벌 (한 벌 = one set/outfit), not 개. Do not confuse 한복 (Korean dress) with 한식 (Korean food).

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'we wear (put on) hanbok (韓服 = Korean traditional dress)'. 입다 specifically covers clothing worn on the torso/body. The phrase describes putting on the full traditional outfit for a celebration or holiday, often the New Year bow (세배) or a major life-event party.

Worn on 설날, 추석, weddings, 돌잔치, and at traditional venues (궁궐). Wearing it is now optional for most — don't assume guests will appear in 한복. Renting a 한복 set (빌리다) for palace photo tours is mainstream and perfectly normal.

입다 (clothes on body) vs 쓰다 (hat/glasses) vs 신다 (shoes) vs 끼다 (ring/glove) vs 차다 (watch). All translate English 'wear' but each covers a specific body region — you cannot use 입다 for shoes, and 신다 for a hanbok gown would be comically wrong.
한복 입다 → 한복 입히다 (dress someone else) → 한복 입고 가다 (go wearing it) → 한복 빌리다 (rent hanbok). Counter: 한 벌 (one set/outfit), 두 벌 (two sets).

Two traps: (1) Using one 'wear' verb for everything — 입다 is only for garments on the body; confusing this leads to 모자를 입어요 (wrong) or 신발을 입어요 (wrong). (2) Counter error — 한복 한 개 is wrong; clothing sets use the counter 벌: 한복 한 벌.

mistakes: Using 입다 for hats/shoes too.
Korean splits 'wear': 옷은 입다, 모자는 쓰다, 신발은 신다. You 입다 a 한복 but 쓰다 a hat and 신다 shoes. Don't use one verb for all.
Saying 한복 입어요 when you mean dressing a child.
To put clothes ON someone else, use the causative 입히다: 애기한테 한복 입혔어요. 입다 is for dressing yourself.
Counting hanbok with 개: 한복 한 개.
Clothing sets take the counter 벌: 한복 한 벌. 개 is for generic objects and sounds wrong for an outfit.

usage: Polite-humble; 드리다 because you give it UP to a parent/elder
When giving DOWN to a child — 주다 (plain give)
세뱃돈 = the cash kids get for their New Year bow
I made sure to slip them some money
챙기다 ('see to/take care of') — warmer, 'I looked after them'
examples: 명절에 부모님께 용돈 드려요.
On holidays I give my parents some money.
Adults giving money to parents — note 께 + 드리다 (honorific direction)
A: 조카들한테 세뱃돈 얼마나 줬어요? / B: 한 명에 오만 원씩 줬어요.
A: How much New Year money did you give your nieces and nephews? / B: I gave 50,000 won to each.
Giving DOWN to children uses 한테 + 주다; 에 + 씩 means 'per person'
할머니가 손주들한테 세뱃돈 주셨어요.
Grandma gave the grandkids their New Year money.
주시다 (honorific of 주다) because Grandma is the respected giver
nuance: On holidays money flows two directions in Korea, and the verb is dictated by the DIRECTION OF RESPECT. 용돈 is 'spending money/allowance'; 세뱃돈 is specifically the cash children receive after giving their 세배 (New Year bow). When YOU give money UP to a parent or elder, use the humble 드리다: 부모님께 용돈 드려요. When you give DOWN to a child or junior, use plain 주다: 조카한테 세뱃돈 줘요. Swapping these is the number-one English-speaker pitfall — 부모님한테 용돈 줘요 is doubly disrespectful (wrong verb AND wrong particle: 한테 is casual, elders take 께). The second contrast is 용돈 (general allowance, any time, including parents) vs 세뱃돈 (only at New Year, tied to the bow, only for children) — adults giving parents holiday money is 용돈, never 세뱃돈. Culturally, adult children giving parents 용돈 at 설날/추석 is a strong filial expectation; the verb 챙기다 ('to see to / not neglect') adds warmth (용돈 챙겨 드렸어요 = 'I made sure to take care of them with money'). Traditional practice: give fresh bills in a clean white envelope.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'I give 용돈 (pocket money/allowance)'. 드리다 ('give humbly to a superior') signals respect upward; 주다 ('give') is the neutral form used downward. The verb is not interchangeable — using the wrong one changes the entire social meaning.

Said at 설날/추석 and at parent-honoring occasions. 드리다 + 께 forms a respectful set when giving to elders; 주다 + 한테 is the casual set for giving to children. Giving parents holiday 용돈 is a strong social expectation — the verb 챙기다 ('see to it') adds warmth.

용돈 (general spending money, any time, including to parents) vs 세뱃돈 (New Year cash, tied to the 세배 bow, only for children — never use 세뱃돈 for money given to parents). The word tells you both the occasion and the generational direction.
용돈 드리다 → 용돈 챙겨 드리다 (thoughtfully take care of / not forget) → 용돈 좀 드렸어요 (gave a little money). For children: 세뱃돈 주다 → 세뱃돈 챙겨 주다 (make sure they get their money).

The number-one trap is 부모님한테 용돈 줘요 — two errors at once: 한테 is casual (elders take 께), and 주다 is plain (elders require humble 드리다). Always pair 께 + 드리다 for upward giving. A second trap: calling any holiday money gift 세뱃돈 — that word is only for children receiving money after the bow.

mistakes: Saying 부모님한테 용돈 줘요.
To a parent/elder, give-up is humble 드리다 and the particle is honorific 께: 부모님께 용돈 드려요. 한테 줘요 is doubly too casual.
Calling the parents' holiday money 세뱃돈.
세뱃돈 is the cash KIDS get for their 세배. Money adults give their parents is 용돈, not 세뱃돈. Match the word to the direction.
Using 드리다 when giving to a child.
드리다 is humble (giving UP). To a child you give DOWN, so use plain 주다: 조카한테 세뱃돈 줬어요. 드리다 to a kid is wrong.

english: How much should I give as a wedding gift?
usage: How much do you give as wedding money?
Polite; asking the going rate, 하다 = 'do/put in' an amount
How much are you putting in?
면 돼요 ('would it be okay to') — asking what's appropriate
How much for the gift money?
부조 = the older general term for congratulatory/condolence money
examples: A: 친한 친구 결혼식인데 축의금 얼마 해요? / B: 친한 친구면 10만 원 이상 해야죠.
A: It's a close friend's wedding — how much should I give? / B: If it's a close friend, you should do at least 100,000 won.
The most natural question-and-advice exchange — closeness is the key variable
요즘은 보통 10만 원 정도 해요.
These days people usually give around 100,000 won.
정도 ('about') — the typical figure for a normal relationship
밥 먹고 가면 좀 더 내는 게 좋아요.
If you stay for the meal, it's better to give a bit more.
A real rule of thumb: attending the buffet means giving more
nuance: 축의금 (祝儀金) is the cash you put in an envelope at a Korean wedding — you almost never bring a wrapped present; you give MONEY at a reception desk. The idiomatic verb is 하다 ('to do', here 'to put in/contribute an amount'): 축의금 얼마 해요? = 'how much do you do as wedding money?'. You can also say 내다 ('to pay/submit') — 축의금 내다 — but 하다 is the most natural when asking the going rate. The amount is socially calibrated: ~5만 원 for an acquaintance, ~10만 원 for a normal friend/colleague, more if you're close or eat at the reception (a real rule: 밥값, 'the meal cost', factors in). An English-speaker pitfall is bringing a physical gift instead of cash — that can be awkward at the reception desk. A second pitfall: Koreans give 'auspicious' figures (3, 5, 7, 10만; avoid 4 because 四 sounds like 死 'death'). The biggest vocabulary trap: do NOT confuse 축의금 (weddings, happy events) with 부의금/조의금 (funerals, condolences) — giving the wrong envelope wording is a grave social error. General umbrella term for both: 부조(금).

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'how much do you 하다 for the wedding money?'. 하다 here means 'to contribute/put in an amount' — a Korean-specific idiom for deciding the gift amount. The whole social act (envelope + cash + amount) is called 축의금 (祝儀金 = congratulatory ceremony money).

Asked among friends or colleagues before a wedding. 얼마 해요? (polite), 얼마 내? (반말). The amount varies by relationship closeness: ~5만 원 (acquaintance), ~10만 원 (normal friend/colleague), more if you attend the meal or are very close. At the reception desk you sign the guestbook (방명록) and hand the envelope.
축의금 (祝儀金, congratulatory — weddings and happy events) vs 부의금/조의금 (弔意金, condolence — funerals). The envelopes, wording, and occasions are opposite; never mix them up. General umbrella term: 부조(금).
축의금 하다 → 축의금 내다 → 부조 하다. The 면 돼요 form (얼마 내면 돼요?) is softer and more deferential. To describe giving it: 축의금 냈어요 ('I gave wedding money').

Two traps: (1) Bringing a physical gift — Korean weddings expect cash in an envelope, not wrapped presents; a gift box at the reception desk is awkward. (2) Using unlucky amounts — avoid any figure with 4 (四 ~ 死); stick to auspicious amounts (3, 5, 7, 10만 원). A third trap: the vocabulary confusion 축의금/부의금 — the wrong word for the wrong ceremony is a serious gaffe.

mistakes: Bringing a wrapped gift instead of cash.
Korean weddings expect 축의금 (money in an envelope) at the reception desk, not presents. A physical gift can be awkward; give cash.
Giving an amount with 4 in it (4만, 14만).
4 (四) sounds like 死 ('death') and is avoided for celebrations. Stick to auspicious figures like 3, 5, 7, or 10만 원.
Confusing 축의금 with 부의금.
축의금 is congratulatory money (weddings, happy events); 부의금/조의금 is condolence money (funerals). The envelopes and wording differ — never mix them up.

usage: Polite default; to the couple or their family
축하드리다 (humble) — more respectful, to elders or formally
I wish you a happy life together
The warm follow-up wish for the newlyweds
examples: 결혼 축하해요! 너무 예쁘다.
Congratulations on your wedding! You look beautiful.
Said to the bride/groom at the hall, with a sincere compliment
두 분 결혼 진심으로 축하드립니다.
I sincerely congratulate you both on your marriage.
진심으로 ('sincerely') + 축하드립니다 for a formal, heartfelt toast or written message
A: 결혼 축하드려요. 신혼여행 어디로 가세요? / B: 감사합니다! 몰디브로 가요.
A: Congrats on the wedding. Where are you honeymooning? / B: Thank you! We're going to the Maldives.
신혼여행 ('honeymoon') — a natural friendly follow-up; note humble 축하드려요 to the couple
nuance: 결혼 축하해요 ('congratulations on your marriage') is the core wedding congratulation. 축하하다 (祝賀) is 'to congratulate', and the politeness ladder matters at a formal event like a wedding: 축하해 (반말, friends only) → 축하해요 (polite, standard) → 축하드려요/축하드립니다 (humble, to elders, the couple's parents, or in a speech). The humble 드리다 form is genuinely common at weddings because you are often congratulating people older than you — the parents at the entrance door. The nearest near-synonym is 결혼 축하드려요: the 드리다 form does NOT change the meaning, only the respect level. The particle pitfall: learners insert 을 (결혼을 축하해요), but the natural set phrase drops it — 결혼 축하해요 (noun directly + 축하하다). Another direct-translation trap: 'congratulations on your wedding' suggests 결혼식 축하해요 ('congrats on the ceremony'), but Koreans congratulate the 결혼 (the marriage), not the event. Warm Korean add-on: 행복하게 잘 살아요 ('live happily together'). Critical rule: 축하하다 is ONLY for joyful occasions — never at a funeral.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'congratulate-하다 (the) marriage'. 축하하다 (祝賀) is a pure 'to congratulate/celebrate', and the object is 결혼 (the state of getting married), not 결혼식 (the ceremony event). The distinction matters — you congratulate the life change, not the party itself.

Said at a 결혼식 (wedding) to the couple, their family, or written in cards. To the couple's parents and any elder guest, use humble 축하드려요/드립니다; to peers use 축하해요; to very close friends 축하해 (반말). Never use 축하 at a funeral — it is strictly for joyful events.

결혼 축하해요 (any well-wisher) vs 결혼 축하드려요 (humble, to an elder couple or parents). Add-on 행복하게 잘 살아요 ('live happily together') is distinctly Korean and very warm — it wishes the marriage itself well, not just the day.
축하해 → 축하해요 → 축하드려요 → 진심으로 축하드립니다. Pair with: 두 분 결혼 (both of you, formal), 행복하게 잘 살아요 (follow-up wish), 신혼여행 잘 다녀오세요 (safe travels on the honeymoon).

Two traps: (1) Inserting 을: 결혼을 축하해요 is slightly stiff/textbook — drop the particle for natural speech: 결혼 축하해요. (2) Object confusion: 'wedding' suggests 결혼식, but Korean targets the marriage (결혼), not the ceremony event. A third trap: saying 축하해요 to the grieving family at a funeral — 축하하다 is only for happiness.

mistakes: Inserting 을: 결혼을 축하해요.
The natural phrase attaches the noun directly: 결혼 축하해요. The 을 isn't wrong grammar but sounds stiff/textbook; drop it for the idiomatic feel.
Using 축하해 with the couple's parents.
축하해 is 반말. To elders (the parents at the wedding) use the humble 축하드려요/축하드립니다, which is standard at formal events.
Saying 축하해요 at a funeral by reflex.
축하하다 is only for joyful occasions. At a funeral it's offensive — use 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 ('may the deceased rest in peace') instead.

english: When are you getting married? (lit. when will you feed us noodles?)
usage: Playful-polite teasing of a dating couple
When are you gonna get married?
언제 국수 먹게 해 줄 거예요?
When do we get to eat your wedding noodles?
Variant with 먹게 해 주다 ('let us eat')
When do we get the wedding noodles?
Said by the friend group, asking collectively
examples: A: 둘이 사귄 지 오래됐는데 국수 언제 먹여 줘요? / B: 아이, 아직 멀었어요!
A: You two have been dating a long time — when's the wedding? / B: Oh, that's still far off!
The classic tease and deflection — the B line 멀었어요 ('still far away') is a very natural reply
국수 먹여 줄 때 됐지!
It's about time you got married!
때 됐지 ('it's about time') — friendly pressure among close friends
국수는 언제쯤 먹을 수 있을까요?
When might we get to eat the wedding noodles?
A gentler, more roundabout version of the same joke — suitable even with semi-formal politeness
nuance: This is an idiom you must not take literally. 잔치국수 (banquet noodles) were traditionally served at wedding feasts, so '국수 먹다' ('to eat noodles') became slang for 'to attend someone's wedding', and 국수 먹여 주다 ('to feed us noodles') means 'to get married'. So 국수 언제 먹여 줘요? = 'when are you two getting married?' — a teasing, affectionate comment directed at a long-term couple. The nearest near-synonym expression is 결혼은 언제 해요? ('when are you getting married?'), which is direct and neutral; 국수 먹여 줘요? is indirect and playful, used only with close friends. The causative chain is key: 먹다 ('eat') → 먹이다/먹여 주다 ('feed someone') — the couple FEEDS (hosts) the noodles and the friends EAT them; getting this backwards breaks the idiom. Register: even the 요 form is inherently playful here; with close friends it's 반말 (먹여 줄 거야?). Social caution: this implies pressure to marry, so use it only with people close enough to joke; saying it to an acquaintance or someone sensitive about being single can feel intrusive. The English-speaker pitfall is total: a 직역 ('when will you feed us noodles?') is baffling in English, and answering about real noodles misses the joke entirely. Compare 잔치 ('feast') — a 돌잔치 is a first-birthday feast, same root.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'when will you feed us noodles?'. Real meaning: 'when are you two getting married?' — because 잔치국수 (banquet noodles) were the traditional wedding feast food, so eating noodles = attending a wedding, and feeding noodles = hosting one. Without knowing this cultural link the sentence makes no sense.

Teasing of a dating couple, typically said by their close friends or family. The 요 form is still playful; full 반말 (먹여 줄 거야?) for very close friends. Social caution: this implies marriage pressure — only say it to people close enough to take the joke. Never to acquaintances or the marriage-sensitive.

국수 언제 먹여 줘요? (when are you getting married?) vs 결혼은 언제 해요? (direct, polite: when are you getting married?). The 국수 version is indirect and teasing; the 결혼 version is direct and more neutral. The noodle idiom is warmer among close friends.
국수 먹여 주다 → 먹여 줄 거야? (반말) → 국수 먹게 해 주다 (variant form) → 우리 언제 국수 먹어요? (group asking). Escalation: 먹여 줄 때 됐지! ('it's time already!') adds stronger teasing pressure.

The pitfall is complete: a 직역 leaves you baffled about noodles and you miss the marriage joke entirely — worse, you might try to answer about actual food. Memorize it as a fixed idiom. A grammar trap: the causative must be 먹여 주다 ('feed someone'), not 먹어 주다 ('eat [for someone]') — the couple feeds, the friends eat.

mistakes: Taking it literally as an offer of food.
국수 먹여 주다 is idiom for 'get married' (from wedding banquet noodles). Don't answer about real noodles — it means 'when's the wedding?'
Saying it to acquaintances or the marriage-sensitive.
It's a tease that implies 'hurry up and marry'. Use only with people close enough to joke; to others it can feel like pressure.
Mangling the causative: 국수 언제 먹어 줘요?
The couple FEEDS the noodles, so it's the causative 먹여 주다 ('feed someone'), not 먹어 ('eat'). 먹여 줘요? = 'when will you feed (treat) us?'

english: My deepest condolences (may the deceased rest in peace)
usage: May the deceased rest in peace
Formal set phrase; the standard thing said/written at a funeral
May the departed rest in peace
Slightly shorter; still formal and correct
I'm at a loss for words
Said directly to the bereaved family, expressing helpless sorrow
A gentler, spoken comfort to a grieving friend (less formal)
examples: 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다.
My deepest condolences.
The phrase you say while bowing at the 빈소, or write on the condolence envelope and funeral wreath — nearly always used as a complete utterance
A: 갑작스러운 비보에 정말 놀랐어요. / B: 정말요. 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다.
A: I was truly shocked by the sudden sad news. / B: Indeed. My deepest condolences.
Natural exchange between two people who both knew the deceased — 비보 ('sad news') opens the condolence naturally
삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다. 얼마나 힘드세요.
My condolences. This must be so hard for you.
After the formal phrase, switch to 얼마나 힘드세요 to comfort the living family — the two serve different purposes
nuance: This is the Korean funeral phrase, and it is almost entirely fixed — memorize it as one unit. Breaking it down: 삼가 ('respectfully/humbly'), 고인 (故人 = 'the deceased'), 명복 (冥福 = 'happiness/blessing in the afterlife'), 빌다 ('to pray/wish') → 'I respectfully pray for the deceased's blessing in the next life'. You say it and write it on the plain white condolence envelope and on funeral wreaths (근조화환) at a 빈소/장례식장. The phrase is for the DECEASED — it is not addressed to the grieving person as a greeting. To the bereaved family you offer 뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없습니다 ('I don't know what to say') or 얼마나 힘드세요 ('how hard this must be for you'). The single biggest English-speaker error is saying 죄송합니다 or 미안해요 as 'I'm sorry (for your loss)' — those mean 'I apologize for a fault' and are completely wrong here. Korean condolence is the 명복을 빕니다 formula. A second pitfall: saying anything cheerful (축하, upbeat 힘내세요 before acknowledging grief). The phrase has no 반말 version; register stays formal throughout. Do not smile; tone is everything.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'I respectfully pray for the deceased's 명복 (冥福 = happiness/blessing in the afterlife)'. 삼가 adds the humble, solemn tone. The phrase directs good wishes toward the soul of the deceased, not toward the living mourner — that distinction is essential.

고인 (故人) = 'the late/deceased person'; 명복 (冥福) = 'blessing in the underworld/afterlife' (冥 = dark/underworld, 福 = blessing); 빌다 = 'to pray/wish'. The Sino-Korean layer makes it formal and irreplaceable with everyday words.

Used exclusively at funerals (장례식장/빈소) — said aloud while bowing, written on condolence envelopes, and inscribed on funeral wreaths. Always formal; no 반말 version exists. The phrase goes toward the DECEASED; to the grieving person you say 얼마나 힘드세요 or 뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없습니다.
chips: 뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없습니다 (to the bereaved)

structuredNuance.t: 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 (for the deceased, always formal) vs 얼마나 힘드세요 (directed at the living mourner, empathetic) vs 뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없습니다 (loss for words, for the bereaved). These serve different recipients — do not conflate them.

The critical trap: translating English 'I'm sorry' as 죄송합니다 or 미안해요 — both mean apologizing for a fault, not condolence. Korean condolence has no apology structure; use 명복을 빕니다. A second trap: using 축하해요 or any cheerful phrase by social reflex. A third: directing 명복을 빕니다 at the living mourner as a greeting — it is only for the deceased.

mistakes: Saying 죄송합니다 or 미안해요 to mean 'sorry for your loss'.
Those mean 'I apologize (for a fault)'. Korean condolence isn't an apology — say 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다, or to the family 뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없습니다.
Saying 축하해요 or anything upbeat by reflex.
축하하다 ('congratulate') is for happy events; at a funeral it's deeply offensive. Keep to the solemn 명복을 빕니다 formula.
Directing 명복을 빕니다 at the living as a hello.
That phrase prays for the DECEASED. To comfort the grieving person, say 얼마나 힘드세요 or 힘내세요; reserve 명복을 빕니다 for the deceased.

usage: What you might murmur handing the envelope; often given silently
How much for the condolence money?
Asking the appropriate amount (부의 = the older term)
I just passed on the condolence money and left
I'll go pay my respects (with money)
부조하다 — the general verb for giving event money
examples: 조의금은 흰 봉투에 넣어서 내요.
Condolence money goes in a plain white envelope.
흰 봉투 ('white envelope') — the required plain envelope for funerals; never use a decorative one
A: 장례식에 직접 못 갔는데 어떻게 하죠? / B: 조의금만 전달해도 괜찮아요.
A: I couldn't attend the funeral — what should I do? / B: It's okay to just send condolence money.
A practical A/B: sending money without attending is socially acceptable
부의금은 보통 5만 원에서 10만 원 정도 해요.
Condolence money is usually around 50,000 to 100,000 won.
The typical range, same avoidance of the number 4 as with wedding money
nuance: 조의금 (弔意金) / 부의금 (賻儀金) is the cash given at a funeral, the solemn counterpart to the wedding 축의금. The verbs: you 내다 ('submit/pay') or 하다 it (조의금 하다, 부조 하다), and if you cannot stay long you 전하다 ('convey/deliver') it. The make-or-break rule for English speakers is the ENVELOPE and its wording: funeral money requires a PLAIN WHITE envelope (흰 봉투) with sober Chinese-character wording — 부의 (賻儀) or 근조 (謹弔). Using a decorative or colorful envelope, or any congratulatory wording (祝), is a grave offense. The cardinal error is carrying over a wedding 축의금 mindset — the verb logic is similar, but tone, envelope, and wording are entirely opposite. Distinguishing the vocabulary: 조의(금) / 부의(금) name the money itself; 근조 is the wording on wreaths and banners ('humbly mourning'). Amounts mirror weddings (~5–10만 원), same avoidance of the number 4. Procedure: sign the 부의록 (condolence guestbook), hand the white envelope quietly, then bow to the portrait. Over-talking is a pitfall — handing the envelope is often done in near silence, and no cheerful speech is needed.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'please receive (accept) the condolence money'. 조의금 (弔意金) = 'money expressing condolence'. The phrase is murmured while handing the white envelope at a 빈소 — it is performative, completing the ritual act of offering rather than starting a conversation.

Used at a 장례식장 (funeral home) or 빈소 (funeral parlour). Give the money quietly at the reception desk: sign the 부의록, hand the plain white envelope, say the phrase (or stay silent) and bow. If you cannot attend, you can 전하다 ('convey/send') the money through someone else — this is acceptable.

조의금 / 부의금 (money label) vs 근조 (written mourning expression, used on wreaths/banners). Compare: 축의금 (wedding money, opposite occasion) — same cash-in-envelope logic but entirely different occasion, envelope style, and wording. Never mix the two up.
조의금 내다 → 조의금 전하다 (send/convey) → 부조 하다 (general: pay respects with money). Asking the rate: 조의금 얼마 해요? / 부의금 얼마 내요?

The cardinal trap is treating condolence money like wedding money — the envelopes are opposite (plain white for funerals vs any for weddings), and the occasion wording reverses completely (근조 / 부의 instead of 祝). A second trap is over-talking: hand the envelope quietly with a bow; a long upbeat speech at a funeral is inappropriate.

mistakes: Using a colored/decorative envelope or 祝 wording.
Funeral money requires a PLAIN WHITE envelope with sober wording (부의/근조). Festive envelopes or 祝('congratulate') are a serious gaffe — that's for weddings.
Calling it 축의금.
축의금 is congratulatory (weddings). Funeral money is 조의금/부의금. The words AND the envelopes are opposite; don't transfer the wedding term.
Giving an amount containing 4.
As with weddings, avoid 4 (四 ~ 死 'death'), which is doubly inappropriate at a funeral. Use figures like 5, 7, or 10만 원.

english: You must be heartbroken (I'm so sorry for your loss)
usage: Polite-honorific; said gently to the bereaved family
How great your sorrow must be
Warmer, more exclamatory version to the mourner
I don't know what words of comfort to offer...
Trailing off — the very Korean way to show you're lost for words
부디 ('please, earnestly') + 힘내세요, a soft encouragement
examples: 상심이 크시겠어요. 부디 힘내세요.
You must be heartbroken. Please stay strong.
The standard two-part comfort: acknowledge grief first, then gently encourage
A: 갑자기 이런 일이... / B: 상심이 크시겠어요. 뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없네요.
A: For this to happen so suddenly... / B: Your grief must be immense. I don't know what to say.
A natural A/B at a 빈소 — A trails off in shock, B responds with empathy and a lost-for-words follow-up
뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없네요. 상심이 크시겠어요.
I'm at a loss for words. You must be heartbroken.
Pairs with 드릴 말씀이 없다 ('no words to offer'), the classic combo at a Korean funeral
nuance: While 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 is addressed about the DECEASED, 상심이 크시겠어요 is what you say TO the grieving family member — and that distinction is exactly what English speakers miss. 상심 (傷心) is 'heartbreak/grief', 크다 ('to be great') in the honorific empathetic form 크시겠어요 ('must be immense for you') → 'your grief must be immense'. The -겠- here is the inferential/empathetic 'must be' (reading the other person's emotion from the outside), and the honorific -시- shows respect to the mourner; both are essential — 상심이 크겠어요 (no -시-) sounds cold. The nearest near-synonym is 얼마나 힘드세요 ('how hard this must be for you'), which is softer and more like 'I see how hard this is'; 상심이 크시겠어요 is slightly more literary. The cardinal pitfall is translating English 'I'm sorry' as 죄송합니다/미안해요 — those apologize for wrongdoing. Korean condolence comfort is indirect and often unfinished: trailing off (뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없네요...) is genuinely more natural and heartfelt than a polished complete sentence. Pair 힘내세요 ('stay strong') AFTER acknowledging the grief — leading with it alone sounds dismissive.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'your 상심 (傷心 = heartbreak/grief) must be great'. The phrase uses the empathetic -겠- form ('must be') plus honorific -시- to gently infer the mourner's feeling and show you see their pain. It addresses the LIVING bereaved person, not the deceased.

Said face-to-face to a grieving family member at a funeral or condolence visit, after bowing and exchanging the standard phrase about the deceased. Keep voice low and tone subdued. There is no 반말 version of this comfort — even to a close friend who is grieving, maintain respectful tone.
chips: 뭐라 위로의 말씀을 드려야 할지... (trailing off)

structuredNuance.t: 상심이 크시겠어요 ('your grief must be immense', more literary) vs 얼마나 힘드세요 ('how hard this must be', softer, broader) vs 뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없습니다 ('I am at a loss for words', the ultimate indirect comfort). All three go to the living mourner, never to pray for the deceased.
상심이 크시겠어요 → 얼마나 상심이 크세요 (warmer, more exclamatory) → (paired with) 부디 힘내세요. The trailing-off variants (뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없네요...) are genuinely the most culturally natural Korean comfort moves.

Two traps: (1) 죄송합니다/미안해요 as 'I'm sorry' — those are apologies for faults, not condolence; they are wrong here. (2) Being too articulate or solution-y ('they're in a better place') — Korean funeral register is restrained sorrow, not problem-solving. Trailing off or short empathy phrases are more appropriate than polished complete sentences.

mistakes: Saying 죄송합니다/미안해요 to mean 'sorry for your loss'.
Those apologize for a fault. To comfort the bereaved, say 상심이 크시겠어요 or 얼마나 힘드세요 — empathy, not apology.
Dropping the honorific -시-: 상심이 크겠어요.
To the grieving family you need -시-: 상심이 크시겠어요. Without it the sympathy sounds detached and under-respectful.
Trying to say something upbeat or 'fix it'.
Korean condolence is restrained and indirect. Trailing off (뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없네요...) is more appropriate than a cheerful or solution-oriented remark.

english: I'd like to invite you to the first-birthday party
usage: I'll invite you to the doljanchi
Polite; the parents inviting guests to the 1st-birthday feast
I'll invite you to the first birthday
Please come to the first-birthday party
Direct invitation with 와 주세요 ('please come')
We've decided to hold a doljanchi
Announcing the plan; 하다 here is fine for 잔치
examples: A: 다음 달에 아기 돌잔치 해요. 초대할게요. / B: 어머, 정말요? 꼭 갈게요!
A: Next month is our baby's first birthday party. I'll invite you. / B: Oh, really? I'll definitely come!
The natural invitation and enthusiastic acceptance — 꼭 갈게요 is the warm reply
돌잔치 와 주실 수 있어요? 돌 반지 안 가져오셔도 돼요.
Can you come to the first birthday? You don't need to bring a gold ring.
돌 반지 ('first-birthday gold ring') — a traditional gift; hosts politely wave it off, but guests often still bring money
주말에 돌잔치라서 정신없었어요.
We had the doljanchi this weekend, so it was hectic.
정신없다 ('hectic/frazzled') — relatable host talk after the event
nuance: 돌잔치 is the celebration of a baby's first birthday (돌 = first birthday + 잔치 = feast/party), a major family event in Korea — historically significant because surviving the first year was once far from certain. 초대하다 (招待) is 'to invite', and 초대할게요 (the -ㄹ게요 intention form) is the host warmly announcing 'I'll invite you / consider yourself on the list.' The highlight ritual is the 돌잡이, where the baby is presented with objects (money, pencil, thread, stethoscope, etc.) and whichever one is grabbed supposedly forecasts the child's future. Gift-wise, the traditional present is a 돌 반지 (a small gold ring) or cash in an envelope (similar logic to 축의금). The English-speaker pitfalls: (1) verb confusion — a 잔치 takes 하다 (돌잔치 하다), which feels inconsistent with memorial rites like 차례 지내다, but for a joyful 잔치/파티 you DO use 하다; 돌잔치 지내다 is wrong. (2) Invite verb — 부르다 ('call/summon') for guests sounds blunt; 초대하다 is the courteous choice. (3) The host disclaimer 돌 반지 안 가져오셔도 돼요 is courtesy — guests typically still bring cash or a small gift. Compare 환갑잔치/칠순잔치 (60th/70th birthday celebrations) — same 잔치 root, for elders.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'I will invite you to the 돌잔치 (first-birthday feast)'. 돌 = the first birthday; 잔치 = feast/party; 초대하다 = to invite (courteously). The -ㄹ게요 signals the speaker's intention/promise: 'I'll make sure to invite you', conveying warmth and inclusion.

Said by new parents to friends, relatives, and colleagues when they're organizing the first-birthday party. 초대할게요 (polite intention) for most adults; 초대할게 (반말) for close friends. The event itself uses 하다: 돌잔치 해요. To describe attending: 돌잔치에 가요.

초대하다 (invite, courteous) vs 부르다 (call/summon, blunt for inviting guests). 돌잔치 하다 (hold the party) vs 차례 지내다 (hold a ritual rite) — the verb differs by occasion: 하다 for celebrations, 지내다 for memorial rites. Compare 환갑잔치 (60th birthday feast) — same 잔치 structure.
초대할게요 → 와 주세요 (please come) → 돌잔치 하기로 했어요 (announcing the plan). Post-event: 돌잔치 잘 됐어요 ('the party went well'). The 돌잡이 ritual is the centerpiece — baby grabs an object, everyone predicts the future.

Three traps: (1) Wrong verb for the event — 돌잔치 지내다 is wrong; use 돌잔치 하다. (2) Wrong invite verb — 부르다 sounds blunt; use 초대하다. (3) Taking the host's 'no gift needed' disclaimer at face value — it's polite deflection; guests typically still bring cash or a small gold gift.

mistakes: Saying 돌잔치 지내요.
지내다 is for ancestral rites (차례/제사). A celebratory party takes 하다: 돌잔치 해요. Save 지내다 for memorial rituals.
Using 부르다 instead of 초대하다 for guests.
부르다 ('call') sounds blunt for inviting people to an event. The courteous verb is 초대하다: 돌잔치에 초대할게요.
Bringing nothing because the host said 'no gift'.
Hosts politely wave off the 돌 반지, but guests typically still give money or a small gold gift. The disclaimer is courtesy, not a literal 'bring nothing'.

english: It's already been a year (said at a first birthday/memorial)
usage: Polite; marveling at how fast the year went, at a 돌잔치
Has it already been a year?
The baby's grown so much already
Cooing over the child's growth at the party
examples: A: 우리 아기 돌잔치예요! / B: 어머, 벌써 일 년이네요. 정말 빨리 컸다!
A: It's our baby's first birthday party! / B: Wow, it's already been a year. They've grown so fast!
The most natural 돌잔치 exchange — -네요 captures the on-the-spot wonder
엊그제 태어난 것 같은데 벌써 일 년이네요.
Feels like she was just born, but it's already been a year.
엊그제 같다 ('feels like just the other day') — the natural partnering sentiment
벌써 일 년이네요. 그동안 키우느라 고생 많으셨어요.
Already a year. You've worked so hard raising her.
고생 많으셨어요 ('you've worked hard') — praising the parents' effort is very Korean
nuance: 벌써 일 년이네요 ('it's already been a year') is a warm, reflective remark perfect for a 돌잔치 (first birthday) — and, in a somber key, for a one-year memorial (일주기). 벌써 means 'already (sooner than expected)', 일 년 is 'one year', and -네요 is the soft exclamatory ending for noticing/realizing something on the spot ('oh, it's already been a year!'). The -네요 is the heart of it: it conveys mild surprise and shared feeling — exactly the register for marveling at how fast a baby's first year flew. The nearest contrast is 벌써 vs 이미: both translate as 'already', but 벌써 carries the emotional 'wow, so soon!' resonance ideal here, while 이미 is flatter and factual ('already done/completed'), so 이미 일 년이네요 loses the warmth. The counting trap: 일 년 uses Sino-Korean 일, and 년 always takes Sino-Korean numbers (일 년, 이 년, 삼 년) — 한 년 (native-Korean number) is wrong. Tone-matching is important: at a happy 돌잔치 this is delighted; the exact same words at a one-year memorial become quietly wistful — read the room. Companion line: 키우느라 고생 많으셨어요 ('you've worked hard raising the child') is very natural added praise for the parents.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'it's already one year, isn't it (-네요)'. The literal reading IS the meaning here — but the emotional weight is in 벌써 ('already, sooner than expected') and -네요 (on-the-spot realization/mild wonder). Together they produce warm, shared amazement at how fast time passed.

Said at a 돌잔치 to the parents, or at a one-year memorial. The polite -네요 form is standard for both contexts. With close friends, drop to 반말: 벌써 일 년이야?. Tone-matching matters: delight at a party, quiet wistfulness at a memorial — the words are the same, but delivery differs completely.

벌써 (already, emotional 'so soon!') vs 이미 (already, neutral/factual). For this warm, marveling moment use 벌써; 이미 일 년이네요 sounds like a flat report. Also: 엊그제 같다 ('feels like just the other day') is a natural companion — the two phrases pair beautifully.
벌써 일 년이네요 → 벌써 이 년이네요 / 삼 년이네요 (two/three years). Add-on praise: 그동안 키우느라 고생 많으셨어요 ('you've worked hard raising them all this time'). Companion: 시간 진짜 빠르네요 ('time really flies').

Two traps: (1) Number error — 년 takes Sino-Korean numbers: 일 년, 이 년, 삼 년. Saying 한 년 (native-Korean numeral) is wrong for the year counter. (2) Dropping -네요 — saying 일 년이에요 is a flat statement of fact with none of the warm on-the-spot amazement; -네요 is what makes the phrase feel alive and socially natural.

mistakes: Using 이미 instead of 벌써.
이미 is flat/factual 'already'; 벌써 carries 'wow, so soon!' emotion. For the warm surprise at a first birthday, say 벌써 일 년이네요, not 이미.
Saying 한 년 instead of 일 년.
The counter 년 takes Sino-Korean numbers: 일 년, 이 년, 삼 년. 한 년 (native number) is incorrect. One year is 일 년.
Dropping -네요 for flat 일 년이에요.
-네요 adds the on-the-spot 'oh, it's already a year!' feeling that fits the moment. Plain 일 년이에요 just states a fact and sounds cold.

english: We go to visit the ancestors' graves
usage: Polite-neutral; the holiday trip to tend ancestors' graves
Are you going to the graves?
We went and visited the graves
갔다 오다 ('went and came back') — reporting it's done
We're going to clear the grave weeds
벌초 = cutting the weeds on the grave before Chuseok
examples: A: 추석에 뭐 해요? / B: 가족이랑 성묘 가요. 할아버지 산소에 절 드리러요.
A: What are you doing for Chuseok? / B: We're going grave-visiting with the family — to bow at Grandfather's grave.
The most natural holiday small-talk exchange — 산소 (honorific grave) and 절 드리다
성묘 가서 할아버지 산소에 절했어요.
We went and bowed at Grandfather's grave.
산소 ('grave', honorific) + 절하다 ('to bow') — the key actions at the grave
요즘은 벌초 대행 서비스 부르는 집도 많아요.
These days many families hire a grave-weeding service.
벌초 대행 ('weeding-by-proxy') — a real modern convenience that shows changing practices
nuance: 성묘 (省墓) is visiting and tending an ancestor's grave, a core part of both 추석 and 설날 — families travel to the gravesite, clean it, set out a little food and drink, and bow (절하다). The verb for the trip is simply 가다: 성묘(를) 가요. To report the trip is done, use 갔다 오다 ('go and come back'): 성묘 갔다 왔어요. A related but distinct word is 벌초 (伐草), specifically cutting the weeds and grass on the grave mound, done shortly before Chuseok — so 성묘 (the respectful visit) and 벌초 (the maintenance work) are different activities. Many busy families now hire a 벌초 대행 service. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) grave vocabulary — use 산소 (honorific term for an ancestor's grave) when speaking of your own family's grave, not the blunt general word 무덤, which feels cold for your own ancestor. (2) The bow at the grave is 절, NOT 세배 — 세배 is only the living New Year bow to elders; confusing them in context is a clear error. (3) Don't 직역 'visit' as 방문하다 — 방문하다 is for visiting people or places socially; for graves the fixed expression is 성묘 가다. Note that Korean burial increasingly uses cremation (화장) with 납골당 (charnel houses), so 성묘 may mean visiting a 납골당 rather than a hillside grave mound.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'I/we go 성묘 (省墓 = visit the grave)'. 성묘 is a Sino-Korean compound: 省 (visit/inspect) + 墓 (grave). The phrase captures the full act of the holiday trip — travel to the gravesite, tidy it, offer food/drink, bow, and leave.

A routine holiday topic during 추석 and 설날 conversations. Plain polite 가요 (성묘 가요) is standard. At the grave, refer to your ancestor's resting place as 산소 (honorific) or 묘, not the generic 무덤. The bow is 절 (not 세배).

성묘 (the respectful visit to pay respects, bow, offer food) vs 벌초 (the practical work of cutting weeds/grass on the grave). They often happen together but are separate activities. Also: 산소 (honorific ancestor's grave) vs 무덤 (generic grave, blunt for a family context).
성묘 가다 → 성묘 갔다 오다 (go and come back) → 성묘 갔다 왔어요 (past, reported). Before the visit: 벌초하러 가다 (go to clear weeds). At the grave: 산소에 절하다 ('bow at the grave'), 술/음식을 올리다 ('offer food/drink').

Three traps: (1) 무덤 instead of 산소 for your own ancestor — 산소 is the respectful, natural choice; 무덤 sounds detached and blunt. (2) 세배 instead of 절 for the grave bow — 세배 is exclusively the living New Year bow to elders; grave bows are 절. (3) 방문하다 instead of 성묘 가다 — 방문하다 is for social visits to living people or places, not for grave visits.

mistakes: Calling your ancestor's grave 무덤.
무덤 is a generic/blunt 'grave'. For your own ancestor use the respectful 산소 or 묘: 할아버지 산소에 성묘 가요.
Saying 세배 for the bow at the grave.
세배 is only the living New Year bow to elders. The bow at a grave (or any ritual bow) is just 절: 산소에서 절했어요.
Using 방문하다 for visiting the grave.
방문하다 is for social visits to people/places. The fixed expression is 성묘 가다 ('go grave-visiting'); 산소를 방문하다 sounds off.

english: I go down to my hometown for the holiday
usage: I go down to my hometown for the holiday
Polite-neutral; the classic holiday travel home
You heading to your hometown for the holiday?
I'm not going home this holiday
The trip home will be jammed
귀성길 = the holiday journey home (notorious traffic)
examples: A: 명절에 고향 내려가요? / B: 네, 부산이 고향이라서 KTX 타고 내려가요.
A: Are you going down to your hometown for the holiday? / B: Yes, my hometown is Busan, so I take the KTX.
The most common holiday small-talk A/B — the answer mentions the hometown and mode of transport
설날에 고향 내려가는데 차 막혀서 다섯 시간 걸렸어요.
Going home for Seollal, traffic made it a 5-hour drive.
차 막히다 ('traffic jams') — the universal holiday-travel complaint;귀성 전쟁 ('going-home war')
이번엔 고향 안 내려가고 그냥 집에서 쉬려고요.
This time I'm not going home, just resting at home.
A natural way to say you're skipping the trip this year
nuance: During 설날 and 추석 most Koreans travel to their family hometown, and the fixed verb is 내려가다 ('to go down') — because Seoul is perceived as 'up' and the provinces as 'down' (a Seoul-centric mental map). You 내려가다 to your 고향 ('hometown') and 올라오다 ('come up') back to Seoul after. The up/down orientation applies even if your hometown is north, east, or west of Seoul — it is about cultural perception, not geography, and this is the key thing English speakers miss when they try 고향에 가요 (fine, but not idiomatic). The holiday exodus is called 귀성 (歸省), and the brutal traffic is 귀성길 ('the road home') / 귀성 전쟁 ('the going-home war') — knowing these makes you sound local. The direction verb matters depending on your position: from Seoul you say 내려가다 ('go down there'); someone already at the hometown says the Seoulite 내려온다 ('comes down here'). The particle 에 is technically correct (고향에 내려가요) but is often dropped in natural speech (고향 내려가요). Don't confuse 고향 ('where you're from / parents' hometown') with 집 ('house/home in the city').

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'I go down to my hometown for the holiday'. The literal reading is the meaning, but 내려가다 ('go down') encodes a Seoul-centric worldview — Seoul is perceived as 'up', the provinces 'down'. Using 올라가다 ('go up') for the provinces would be backwards.

A universal holiday conversation topic. Polite 내려가요 (standard for colleagues, acquaintances); 내려가? (반말, friends). The counter-phrase for staying: 고향 안 내려가요. Asking about traffic is natural: 귀성길 많이 막혔어요? ('Was the road home very jammed?')

고향에 가요 ('I go to my hometown', neutral/correct but flat) vs 고향 내려가요 (idiomatic, Seoul-centric, what natives actually say). 고향 ('hometown/region of origin') vs 집 ('house in the city') — for the holiday journey the word is 고향, not 집.
명절에 고향 내려가다 → 고향 안 내려가다 (not going) → 고향 갔다 오다 (went and came back). Return to Seoul: 올라오다 / 올라왔어요 ('came back up'). Traffic talk: 귀성길 막히다 ('road home jammed'), 귀성 전쟁 ('going-home war').

Two traps: (1) Direction reversal — 고향에 올라가요 ('I go UP to my hometown in the provinces') is backwards; the provinces are always 'down'. Saying 올라가요 to mean heading out of Seoul signals you don't know the Seoul-centric map. (2) 집 vs 고향 — 집 is your city apartment; 고향 is the ancestral hometown you travel to for the holidays. 집에 내려가요 makes no sense for this.

mistakes: Saying 고향에 올라가요 to mean going home to the provinces.
From Seoul you go DOWN to the provinces: 내려가요. 올라가요 ('go up') is for heading toward Seoul. The up/down is Seoul-centric, not compass-based.
Mixing 내려가다 and 내려오다.
Use 내려가다 ('go down there') when you're in Seoul heading to the hometown. 내려오다 ('come down here') is from the hometown's viewpoint. Direction depends on where you are.
Translating 'hometown' as 집.
집 is your house/home; 고향 is the region you're from / your parents' place. For the holiday journey it's 고향 내려가요, not 집에 내려가요.
